rv.q: What's real in Tom Stoppard's 'The Real Thing' is the exquisite pleasure of hearing his language spoken by actors who understand its music.
A thoroughly excellent and tuneful version of Tom Stoppard's brilliant play about love and fidelity.
True to form, The Real Thing (1982) is exceedingly well made, a keen and touching study of fidelity, fiction and marital love among theater folk.
Mr. Lloyd and Ms. McNeal are both superb, bringing fresh life to characters.
This revival is a thoughtful, well-acted production that finds fresh currents in familiar waters.

The less brittle characterizations and less distant tone invite a search for deeper meaning that the script is rightfully loath to cough up.
But pretty much everything else in Sam Gold‘s hollow revival is a little off.
The witty word-play and posturing quickly grew tired and the characters rarely transcended their arch banter.
Out of this cat’s cradle comes a dissection of the byways of desire that finds neither Gyllenhaal nor McGregor ideally cast.
Helmer Sam Gold’s mannered production is so steeped in artifice, it’s almost antagonistic to the text.
Gold's playful, musical but strangely inert Broadway revival adds unnecessary layers of artifice, dulling its crucial sense of danger.
Tom Stoppard's 1982 play about love, marriage and the nature of art gets a handsome but lifeless revival that squanders a terrific cast.
There can be power and beauty in forthright expression, as this stirring revival reminds us.
Some people find Tom Stoppard's writing not much more than brain candy but the brilliance of this eloquent writer is his ability to go beyond the head straight to the heart.
A terrific cast led by McGregor has triumphed with it yet again.

Not only is it harder to follow the tricky plot (and its plays-within-plays), but the songs suggest a kumbaya solidarity among the characters that undercuts the show's message about the challenges of forging connections.
But “The Real Thing” is still looking good.
This revival isn’t perfect, but McGregor and Gyllenhaal are definitely the real thing.
This production sacrifices the pleasant strengths of The Real Thing while exposing its flaws.

Under the direction of Sam Gold, the current Broadway revival of Tom Stoppard's The Real Thing is a messy, unfocused production that wastes the considerable talents of Ewan McGregor and Maggie Gyllenhaal.
A thoroughly excellent and tuneful version of Tom Stoppard's brilliant play about love and fidelity.

The actors are superb, but this is not “The real thing.”
Despite the somewhat off-kilter staging, Stoppard’s dazzling wit and compassion shine through.
